name: FatPipe Networks
evidence_summary: FatPipe sources evidence SD-WAN, dynamic load balancing, native security, application QoS, WAN optimisation and cloud-enabled SD-WAN.
cost_model: Quote-based appliances/software/support; public price transparency limited.
key_differentiators: Long heritage in WAN optimisation, dynamic load balancing and MPSec encryption.
Independent vendor offering platform flexibility without lock-in to a larger ecosystem.
Application QoS and traffic shaping capabilities are mature.
best_fit_for: Mid-market organisations wanting SD-WAN without the operational overhead of larger platform vendors.
Buyers prioritising load balancing and WAN performance over full SASE convergence.
Specific use cases requiring native WAN optimisation as part of the SD-WAN platform.
watch_outs: Significantly smaller vendor than the category leaders; ecosystem, partner channel and roadmap velocity should be confirmed.
SASE and SSE capabilities are not primary positioning; security relies on partner integration.
Public pricing and case study transparency are limited; expect more discovery work in evaluation.
verification_notes: Re-verified 2026-07-29 against named primary sources. Every graded fact carries a source, a tier and a verbatim quote confirmed present on the cited page by an independent check. Industry, region, organisation-size and pricing evidence was sourced on the same basis. Facts that could not be sourced are published as unknown with the reason. The value_tier field is a Netify assessment of relative cost position, not a supplier claim: most of this market publishes no price. Sources found and rejected are listed at tier 4.

ai_capability.note: No public evidence of AI capability reviewed.

resilience.note: MPVPN multi-path WAN redundancy by design; HA appliance pairs.

profile.platform_architecture: FatPipe pioneered router-clustering and multipath WAN technology, with patents in the space stretching back two decades. Its MPVPN and related appliances aggregate multiple WAN links with per-packet load balancing, failover and WAN path control, deployable without changing existing routers. Management is via FatPipe's central console. The company is US-based with deployments in government, finance and healthcare.
profile.security_sase: Security capability covers encryption across aggregated paths, firewalling and integration patterns with third-party security stacks; there is no first-party SASE cloud. Public evidence of AI capability was not confirmed in our review. Buyers needing ZTNA, SWG, CASB or DLP should plan a dual-vendor design with an SSE provider.
profile.service_support_channel: Channel and direct sales with support contracts; UK presence is lighter than the major vendors, so confirm local delivery and support arrangements during procurement. Reference verticals include public sector and healthcare in North America and India.
profile.commercials_verdict: Appliance plus support licensing, quote based, typically competitive. The Netify verdict: consider FatPipe where multi-link aggregation and link-state independence from carriers is the specific problem, or where its patents-led approach matches an existing estate. For most UK enterprise SASE shortlists, mainstream platforms with deeper local channel and security stacks will rank ahead; our evidence coverage for FatPipe is lower, so verify claims via RFP.

vendor_faqs.q: What problem does FatPipe MPVPN solve?
vendor_faqs.a: It aggregates multiple WAN links from different carriers into one logical path with per-packet balancing and instant failover, without BGP complexity or carrier cooperation, which appeals where uptime requirements exceed what one provider can offer.
No. It is WAN reliability and path control technology. Pair it with a cloud security platform for ZTNA, SWG, CASB and DLP if you need SASE outcomes.

vendor_faqs.q: How strong is FatPipe's UK support?
vendor_faqs.a: Presence is lighter than mainstream vendors. Ask for named UK support arrangements, response SLAs and local references as part of any evaluation; our review graded several dimensions unknown for lack of public evidence.

shortlist_summary: FatPipe bring long heritage in WAN optimisation, dynamic load balancing and MPSec encryption, pre-dating the SASE category and focused on those specific capabilities rather than a full SASE security stack. Typically shortlisted by organisations with particular multi-path WAN optimisation or encryption requirements where that established specialism matters more than broader SASE convergence.
cost_note: Appliance plus support licensing, competitively priced; a specialist value play for multipath WAN.
uk_basis: No UK HQ (US). UK delivery would be via partners; confirm local support during procurement.

f01_fully_managed_service.quote: To proactively manage and troubleshoot WAN connectivity, there is a single point-of-contact that leads to increased network redundancy.
f01_fully_managed_service.note: FatPipe publishes a Managed WAN Edge solution page describing proactive management, a single point of contact, zero-touch provisioning and 24x7x365 device health monitoring, which is more than a pure product play. However no page reviewed states that FatPipe designs, deploys, makes changes, supports and reports end to end, and no service description or support policy was found (the technical support page is a feedback form only). Graded partial on that basis.

f03_co_managed_service.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. The Managed WAN Edge page, Orchestrator page, EnterpriseView page and technical support page contain no statement of shared responsibility, customer-retained change rights or a co-managed operating model. Absence is not being treated as a no.

f04_multi_tenant_msp_white_label_support.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. The Orchestrator page returned no occurrences of multi-tenant, tenant, MSP, managed service provider, white label, branding or delegated administration; EnterpriseView and Detailed Network Visibility likewise. The partners page is distribution oriented (Carahsoft, TD SYNNEX, CDW, deal registration) and does not describe white-label operation. No partner portal or MSP documentation was reachable.

f05_professional_services_and_migration_.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. No professional services, deployment services, migration, discovery, pilot, runbook, rollback or training page was found on the site; the about and company pages returned HTTP 404 and the support page carries only a feedback form.

f07_lifecycle_management.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. The Orchestrator page contains no firmware upgrade or patching statement, the technical support page publishes no RMA, warranty or hardware replacement terms, and the Managed WAN Edge page does not say lifecycle tasks are included in the service. Zero-touch provisioning is described but that is deployment, not lifecycle.

f17_cellular_and_5g_support.quote: Enables seamless cellular connectivity via an external 5G modem or embedded SIM, offering flexible deployment options for secure, scalable, and efficient network management.
f17_cellular_and_5g_support.note: Vendor claim, well supported. The 5G and LTE page also states that cellular links can serve as automatic failover paths or as primary connections when wired broadband is not available, describes single-SIM instant failover, and says administrators can manage LTE or 5G data usage by policy. The Managed WAN Edge page lists 4G/5G among monitored link types. Signal-strength monitoring specifically was not found, though link monitoring of 4G/5G is stated.

f19_public_cloud_gateways.quote: SD-WAN Branches connect to the nearest SASE point of presence (PoP), which applies security and routing policies dynamically.
f19_public_cloud_gateways.note: FatPipe describes its own SASE PoPs and states the solution is deployed through FatPipe's cloud-based security layer, which points to vendor-operated infrastructure rather than a resold third party, and no third-party gateway vendor is named on any page read. Graded partial rather than yes because FatPipe publishes no PoP location list, count or map, and no page states who owns or hosts the PoPs. No evidence was found that would justify partner_integrated either.

f20_private_pops_dedicated_pops.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. The SASE page refers to on-premise intelligence alongside the cloud security layer but never offers a customer-hosted, dedicated or sovereign PoP deployment. No sovereignty or dedicated-instance page was found.

f21_private_global_backbone.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. No page read contains any backbone, private network core or inter-region transit claim. The MPVPN and WARP products bond customer internet and ISP lines rather than riding a FatPipe-owned network, but that is context, not proof that no backbone exists.

f26_sla_backed_service_fabric.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. FatPipe publishes several achievable WAN reliability figures on marketing pages but no service level agreement document, no uptime commitment, no response or change-handling targets, and no latency, jitter or loss commitments. The technical support page publishes no response times. See the conflicts list for the differing reliability percentages.

f27_integrated_next_generation_firewall.quote: FatPipe Cloud Security includes essential capabilities such as IPS and web filtering, DNS protection, SSL inspection, antimalware, ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access), endpoint protection, Secure Web Gateway (SWG), antivirus, and antispam.
f27_integrated_next_generation_firewall.note: Vendor claim. The Secure Connectivity page states FatPipe has native inbuilt capabilities providing stateful firewall, DDoS protection, advanced web filtering and intrusion detection and prevention, and the Total Security 360 page states the firewall acts as the first line of defense with built-in IPS functionality. Application classification and control is a separately published SD-WAN feature. No third-party firewall vendor is named on any page read, so graded yes rather than partner_integrated.

f33_data_loss_prevention.quote: Additionally, FatPipe integrates Data Loss Prevention (DLP) at the data layer, inspecting outbound packets to detect and block sensitive information such as credit card or social security numbers from leaving the organization.
f33_data_loss_prevention.note: Vendor claim, presented as FatPipe's own capability with no third-party DLP engine named. Inspection and blocking of outbound sensitive data before it leaves the organisation is explicit. The alerting and exception or incident workflow element of the definition is not described on any page read, so confidence is medium rather than high.

f40_managed_service_assurance.quote: FatPipe edge device health is monitored 24x7x365.
f40_managed_service_assurance.note: Round-the-clock proactive monitoring with automated email and SMS alerting is published, which covers part of the definition. Graded partial because no page read names a NOC or SOC, states that FatPipe owns incidents through to root cause analysis, or describes structured service reviews or change governance. EnterpriseView contains no NOC, 24/7 or root cause references.

delivery_model.quote: FatPipe edge device health is monitored 24x7x365.
delivery_model.note: FatPipe is primarily a technology vendor authoring its own appliances and software (MPVPN, WARP, Total Security 360, Orchestrator, EnterpriseView) and sells through distributors named on its partner page (Carahsoft, TD SYNNEX, CDW). It also publishes a Managed WAN Edge solution page describing 24x7x365 device health monitoring and a single point of contact, so a service-operator role is claimed as well. Graded both, medium confidence, because no service description, service catalogue or contract terms were found to confirm the depth of the managed offer.

underlay_ownership.quote: FatPipe WARP achieves fault tolerance for companies by creating an easy method of combining two or more Internet connections of any kind over multiple ISPs.
underlay_ownership.note: FatPipe's products bond and steer connections the customer already has from multiple ISPs, and the WARP page states the product works with your existing infrastructure. No page read offers FatPipe-supplied circuits, carrier services or an owned routing core, and no access portfolio or price list was found. Graded customer_supplied_only at medium confidence because the absence of a connectivity offer is inferred from the pages read rather than stated outright.

sse_layer_ownership.quote: FatPipe Cloud Security includes essential capabilities such as IPS and web filtering, DNS protection, SSL inspection, antimalware, ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access), endpoint protection, Secure Web Gateway (SWG), antivirus, and antispam.
sse_layer_ownership.note: Every security function is branded as FatPipe's own (FatPipe Cloud Security, FatPipe ZTNA, FatPipe Firewall-as-a-Service, FatPipe IPS, FatPipe SIEM) and the Secure Connectivity page claims native inbuilt firewall, DDoS, web filtering and IDS/IPS. No OEM or partner security vendor is named on any page read. Confidence is medium because this rests entirely on vendor self-description, with no OEM disclosure, engine attribution or third-party test report available.

regulatory_documentation.quote: FatPipe appliances use FIPS Compliant encryption with IPSec and GRE encapsulation, ensuring strong security and compliance with industry standards for safe data transmission.
regulatory_documentation.note: Frameworks found named on the site: FIPS, but only as 'FIPS Compliant encryption' with no certificate number or CMVP validation reference; and HIPAA, PCI DSS and GDPR on the SIEM and compliance page, where they appear as customer compliance-reporting features of the SIEM product rather than attestations held by FatPipe. Frameworks NOT found anywhere: ISO 27001, SOC 2, NIS2, DORA, NHS DSPT, Cyber Essentials. No trust centre, certification register entry or attestation report was found, and the privacy policy and about URLs returned HTTP 404. Graded assurance_only accordingly.

pop_count.note: Not found in public sources reviewed. The SASE page refers to branches connecting to the nearest SASE point of presence but gives no total, no list of PoP cities or regions and no coverage map. No PoP count appears on the homepage, the Remote User Connectivity page or any other page read.

sla_availability_pct.note: Not found in public sources reviewed as a service level agreement figure. FatPipe publishes several different achievable WAN reliability or availability marketing figures across its pages (99.98%, 99.999%, 99.9998% and 99.999988%) but these are product performance claims, not a contractual availability commitment, and no SLA document, support policy or service credit scheme was found. The figures also disagree with one another, so no single value can be reported; see conflicts.

sectors.healthcare.quote: FatPipe's software solutions have been deployed by over 2,500 end-user customers across a diverse set of sectors including education, financial services, government, healthcare, hospitality, legal, manufacturing, retail, and transportation and in various deployment models, including hybrid, SaaS, and managed services.
sectors.healthcare.note: Named in the SEC 10-K sector list and backed by a dedicated healthcare case study PDF (source 10) describing a benefits and medical claims processor operating between California and Texas under HIPAA and COBRA obligations. The case study customer is anonymised, so there is no named healthcare reference account. Homepage case study strapline reads 'Delivering reliable MPVPN connectivity for healthcare operations and patient data security.'

sectors.financial_services.quote: It is designed for organizations that depend on secure, high-performance connectivity, such as financial institutions, credit unions, retailers, restaurant chains, logistics companies, and multi-branch enterprises.
sectors.financial_services.note: Three independent supplier sources: the SEC 10-K sector list names 'financial services'; the MPVPN product page names financial institutions and credit unions (quoted here); and a dedicated case study PDF (source 15) covers 'one of the leading mortgage financing companies in Rhode Island'. Customer anonymised. No banking accreditation or regulatory framework page found.

sectors.retail_ecommerce.quote: A leading retail company provides thousands of products to the market through 40+ store locations plus 10 distribution centers.
sectors.retail_ecommerce.note: Quote is from the dedicated retail case study PDF (source 14). Corroborated by the SEC 10-K sector list, by the MPVPN page naming retailers, and by the SASE page: 'Industries like retailers can embrace FatPipe SASE framework and integrate secure web gateway (SWG), zero trust network access, and cloud access security broker (CASB) straight into their network architecture.' Evidence is bricks-and-mortar retail and point of sale connectivity, not ecommerce; no ecommerce-specific evidence was found.

sectors.manufacturing.quote: A large Europe-based packaging manufacturer that relies heavily on its Internet connectivity for business
sectors.manufacturing.note: Quote is from the dedicated manufacturing case study PDF (source 13), which also states 'The company is globally distributed with offices in Europe, Asia, and North America.' Corroborated by the SEC 10-K sector list. Customer anonymised. Homepage strapline: 'Optimizing WAN performance across manufacturing plants and supply chains.'

sectors.energy_utilities.quote: For public sector customers, FatPipe helps agencies, schools, libraries, healthcare organizations, utilities, and local governments maintain connectivity when a carrier, circuit, or site connection fails.
sectors.energy_utilities.note: Graded unknown deliberately. Utilities appear only in this sentence on the Carahsoft reseller page, which is a tier 3 source and under the tier rules cannot carry a grade alone. Energy and utilities is absent from the SEC 10-K sector list, absent from the homepage case study set (which covers ten other verticals), and absent from the MPVPN and SASE pages. Checked: homepage case study index, all nine case study PDFs, 10-K, MPVPN page, SASE page, TS360 page, partners page. No utility, energy, oil and gas, or OT/ICS material found.

sectors.government_public_sector.quote: A US Tax Court has recently added FatPipe WARP to futureproof their network from increased online demand due to the Covid-19 lockdown.
sectors.government_public_sector.note: Strongest sector evidence in the set. A named institution type (a US Tax Court) in source 17; a separate Cities and Counties case study (source 16) covering a contractor to the US Department of Defense; the SEC 10-K sector list naming 'government'; and a public sector distribution route via Carahsoft, described on FatPipe's own partners page as 'Carahsoft is The Trusted IT Solutions Provider®, supporting Federal, State, Local Government, Education, Healthcare, and Private Sector industries.' No specific contract vehicle or FedRAMP/GSA schedule number was published on either the FatPipe or Carahsoft page.

sectors.education.quote: An international school system has over 500 schools within its boundaries.
sectors.education.note: Quote is from the dedicated education case study PDF (source 12), headed 'CASE STUDY EDUCATION'. Corroborated by the SEC 10-K sector list and by the Carahsoft public sector route naming Education. Customer anonymised and no country stated, so the deployment geography for this reference is not established.

sectors.transport_logistics.quote: The transportation company, a prominent temperature-controlled carrier, provides comprehensive range of transportation solutions to fulfill the demands of a growing customer base.
sectors.transport_logistics.note: Quote is from the dedicated transport case study PDF (source 18). Corroborated by the SEC 10-K sector list ('transportation') and the MPVPN page naming 'logistics companies'. Customer anonymised; the PDF refers to a 'global network' but names no country.

sectors.professional_services.quote: FatPipe's software solutions have been deployed by over 2,500 end-user customers across a diverse set of sectors including education, financial services, government, healthcare, hospitality, legal, manufacturing, retail, and transportation and in various deployment models, including hybrid, SaaS, and managed services.
sectors.professional_services.note: Graded partial, not yes. 'Legal' is named in the SEC 10-K sector list and FatPipe runs a Legal vertical on its homepage, but the only supporting case study is a US Tax Court, which is a judicial body and has been counted under government_public_sector instead. No law firm, accountancy, consultancy or other professional services firm case study or reference was found. Homepage strapline for the Legal vertical is court-focused: 'Network solutions for courts and legal institutions requiring high availability.'

sectors.hospitality_leisure.quote: The destination resort is one of the most prominent and famous establishments on Las Vegas Boulevard.
sectors.hospitality_leisure.note: Quote is from the dedicated hospitality case study PDF (source 11), whose filename references 'Stratosphere' although the customer is not named in the document text. Corroborated by the SEC 10-K sector list ('hospitality') and by the MPVPN page naming 'restaurant chains'. Homepage strapline: 'Achieving network resilience and uptime for hospitality and entertainment venues.'

regions.uk_ireland.quote: We service customers in geographies around the world, with our largest customer populations located in the United States and India.
regions.uk_ireland.note: No UK or Ireland evidence found. Checked: the Contact page, which lists exactly five corporate locations (Salt Lake City USA, Chennai India, Makati Philippines, Midrand South Africa, Huntingdale Australia) and no UK or Irish entity; the SEC 10-K, which mentions no UK, Ireland or Europe revenue or operations; the partners page, which names Carahsoft, TD SYNNEX and CDW without stated territories; and the SASE page, which references a 'nearest SASE point of presence (PoP)' but publishes no PoP list. A generic 'geographies around the world' claim is not treated as UK coverage.

regions.europe.quote: A large Europe-based packaging manufacturer that relies heavily on its Internet connectivity for business
regions.europe.note: Graded partial on the strength of a single published customer deployment for a Europe-headquartered manufacturer (source 13), which also states 'The company is globally distributed with offices in Europe, Asia, and North America.' Against this: FatPipe has no European office or legal entity on its Contact page, the SEC 10-K names no European revenue or operations and lists expansion targets as North America, Southeast Asia, Mexico and India only, and no European PoP locations are published anywhere. This is customer-side evidence of a deployment, not published European service coverage.

regions.north_america.quote: Our revenues are primarily generated in the United States, with India generating an increasing share of sales since 2022.
regions.north_america.note: SEC-filed statement of revenue geography, the strongest region evidence available. Reinforced by the Salt Lake City headquarters ('392 East Winchester Street, Salt Lake City, UT 84107'), by named US deployments (a US Tax Court, a Rhode Island mortgage financier, a US Department of Defense support contractor), by US public sector distribution through Carahsoft and CDW, and by the 10-K statement 'We plan to continue expanding our presence throughout North America and parts of Southeast Asia.' Evidence is United States specific; nothing Canada or Mexico specific was found beyond a stated plan to expand into Mexico.

regions.asia_pacific.quote: We service customers in geographies around the world, with our largest customer populations located in the United States and India.
regions.asia_pacific.note: India is the second largest customer base per the SEC 10-K, and the majority of the workforce is there: the filing reports 172 full-time staff, '56 in the United States, 112 in India, and 4 in the Philippines.' Three APAC legal entities are published on the Contact page: FatPipe Networks Pvt Ltd (Chennai, India), FatPipe Networks Inc (Makati, Philippines) and FatPipe Networks Australia Pty Ltd (Huntingdale, VIC). The 10-K also states 'We are currently exploring options to grow our global sales, with emphasis on expansion opportunities within the burgeoning India information technology market.' Note this is India-centred; no Japan, Korea or Singapore evidence was found, and Southeast Asia is described as prospective.

regions.middle_east_africa.note: Graded partial and low confidence. The only evidence is a South African office address on the Contact page under the entity name 'FatPipe Networks Inc' with phone numbers +27 11 318 4700 and +27 82 441 9238. That establishes corporate presence, not published service delivery: the SEC 10-K does not list South Africa among operating locations (it names only the US, India and the Philippines) and reports no African revenue. Conflict noted rather than resolved: the marketing site shows a South African office the 10-K does not account for. No Middle East evidence of any kind was found.

regions.latin_america.quote: We plan to expand its presence in Mexico and Asia markets with products and services bundles to address geography specific markets.
regions.latin_america.note: Graded unknown. The only Latin America reference in any source is this forward-looking expansion intention in the SEC 10-K, which is a plan and not current delivery. No Latin American office, entity, partner, PoP, case study or Spanish or Portuguese language coverage page was found. Checked: Contact page, partners page, 10-K, homepage case study set.

regions.china_mainland.quote: We are in discussions with multiple potential partners in Southeast Asia, which does not include China, to address these local markets.
regions.china_mainland.note: Unusually strong negative evidence: the SEC 10-K explicitly carves China out of its Asian partner strategy. China otherwise appears in the filing only in risk factor language about geopolitical tension ('Rising tensions between China and Taiwan'). No mainland China ICP licence, PoP, partner or entity was found. The homepage '10K+ Customers Worldwide' claim is treated as evidence of nothing here.

organisation_fit.large_global_enterprise.quote: The Company's end-user customers range in size from smaller businesses to Fortune 1000 enterprise users, but its core customer base can be classified as mid-market companies.
organisation_fit.large_global_enterprise.note: Graded partial rather than yes on the supplier's own SEC-filed wording: Fortune 1000 users exist at the top of the range but are explicitly not the core base. Supporting deployments of scale include an international school system with over 500 schools and a US Department of Defense support services contractor. The 10-K also describes FatPipe as 'a leading developer of enterprise-class, application-aware, secure SD-WAN solutions and integrated single-stack cybersecurity solutions for organizations, including enterprises, communication service providers, security service providers, government organizations, and other middle-market companies.' No named global enterprise logo, no enterprise product tier and no global 24x7 support commitment page was found.

organisation_fit.mid_market.quote: The Company's end-user customers range in size from smaller businesses to Fortune 1000 enterprise users, but its core customer base can be classified as mid-market companies.
organisation_fit.mid_market.note: The clearest organisation fit signal for this supplier and the one to lead with. Independently corroborated by Info-Tech Research Group / SoftwareReviews, whose midmarket-specific SD-WAN category FatPipe has topped repeatedly. Award labels on the supplier's own page read '2026 Data Quadrant Champion SD-WAN Midmarket', '2025 Emotional Footprint Champion SD-WAN Midmarket', '2024 Data Quadrant Champion SD-WAN Midmarket' and '2023 Data Quadrant Champion SD-WAN Midmarket', drawn 'From 59 validated reviews on SoftwareReviews.' The 10-K restates the same finding, so the analyst claim is attested in an SEC filing.

organisation_fit.small_business.quote: The Company's end-user customers range in size from smaller businesses to Fortune 1000 enterprise users, but its core customer base can be classified as mid-market companies.
organisation_fit.small_business.note: Graded partial. Smaller businesses are stated to be within the customer range but there is no SMB product tier, no SMB pricing, no self-service purchase route and no small business case study. The TS360 page uses only generic language, 'Every business, irrespective of their size, is challenged with their own share of vulnerabilities due to their weaker security postures.' The 10-K contains a risk factor arguing the opposite way, warning that 'the market perception that all-in-one solutions may be suitable only for small and medium-sized businesses because such solution lacks the performance capabilities and functionality of other solutions may harm our sales to large businesses, service provider and government organization end-customers', which indicates the company is positioning away from an SMB-only perception rather than towards SMB.

published_pricing.note: No price is published that we could quote. The value_tier field on this record is a Netify assessment of relative cost position, not a supplier claim.
